The giant stargazer Kathetostoma giganteum, an ambush predator inhabiting the continental shelf of New Zealand and southern Australia, exhibits a life history characterized by slow growth and considerable longevity. Recent growth studies indicate that individuals ultimately attain a standard length of 90 cm [Li = 90 cm], making it one of the larger members of the Uranoscopidae family. This maximum size is accompanied by a substantial ultimate wet body mass of approximately 13.3 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 13.3 kilograms], a value derived from length–weight relationships for the species. Such dimensions imply a prolonged juvenile phase before the onset of maturation, as the energetic demands of reaching this size are considerable within the temperate waters of its range.

During the initial stages of development, the species produces relatively small offspring. Based on an observed egg diameter of 2.3 mm, the estimated wet weight at birth for the newly emerged yolk-sac larva is 0.0064 grams [Wwb = 0.0064 grams]. This modest initial mass, characteristic of a planktonic larval phase, necessitates a period of rapid growth in the upper water column to reduce vulnerability to predation. However, under the consistently cool thermal regime of the species' habitat, measured at 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C], the metabolic rate of these early life stages is constrained, leading to a relatively protracted larval duration when compared to warmer-water congeners, which influences overall recruitment success.

The transition to reproductive maturity is marked by a notable size threshold. Puberty, defined as the standard length at which gonadal recrudescence is initiated, occurs at 47.5 cm [Lp = 47.5 cm] for K. giganteum. This measurement correlates with a wet weight at puberty of 1.93 kilograms [Wwp = 1.93 kilograms], representing roughly fifteen percent of the species' ultimate mass. Attaining this size requires several years of benthic existence, during which the fish establishes a territory on the seafloor. The onset of vitellogenesis in females at this body mass suggests a significant energetic investment is necessary before the first reproductive event can be supported by available prey resources.

Under the stable thermal conditions of 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C], an adult female K. giganteum is capable of producing approximately 1,417 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1,417 eggs per spawning event] and spawns approximately once per year [F_R_i = spawns approximately once per year]. This strategy, producing numerous small pelagic eggs, is typical of demersal spawners that rely on broad dispersal for offspring survival rather than extended parental care, an adaptation to the relatively stable but unproductive deep-reef environment.

Longevity data for K. giganteum indicate a remarkable lifespan when compared to many other teleosts. The maximum recorded life span for the species, observed in wild populations at an ambient water temperature of 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C], is 20 years [am = 20 years]. This substantial life span, combined with its delayed maturity and large ultimate body size, places K. giganteum firmly within a slow life-history continuum. Such a strategy is likely an adaptive response to low natural mortality rates in the adult stage, where the species faces few predators due to its formidable size and venomous opercular spines, and where the energetic costs of rapid growth are traded for a longer, more stable reproductive window.
